**Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) – General Overview** | Category | Key Points | |----------|------------| | **What it is** | Vitamin B12 is a water‑soluble B‑vitamin essential for DNA synthesis, red‑blood‑cell formation, and normal nervous‑system function. | | **Common Forms** | • **Cyanocobalamin** – synthetic, inexpensive, long‑lasting.
• **Methylcobalamin** – the naturally occurring form found in food.
• **Hydroxocobalamin** – often used in injections and has a longer half‑life. | | **Routes of Administration** | • **Oral tablets or capsules** – most common for general supplementation.
• **Sublingual tablets or sprays** – absorbed under the tongue.
• **Intramuscular (IM) injection** – used for severe deficiency or malabsorption (e.g., pernicious anemia). | | **Typical Dosages** | • **Oral**: 250 µg–1 000 µg daily for deficiency or maintenance.
• **Sublingual**: 500 µg–1 000 µg daily.
• **IM**: 1000–2000 µg once weekly for several weeks, then maintenance dose (e.g., 1000 µg monthly). Dosage varies with age, sex, pregnancy, and the underlying cause. | | **When It’s Used** | • **Vitamin B12 deficiency** (fatigue, anemia, neuropathy).
• **Pernicious anemia** (autoimmune gastritis).
• **Digestive disorders** (celiac disease, Crohn’s disease) that impair absorption.
• **Certain medications** (metformin, proton‑pump inhibitors) that reduce B12 uptake.
• **Dietary restriction** (strict vegans/vegans) – supplementation often required. | | **Common Side Effects** | Very rare; may include mild rash, itching, or dizziness. High doses (thousands of micrograms) are generally safe; B12 is excreted in urine if taken in excess. | | **Drug Interactions** | • Metformin, proton‑pump inhibitors, H2 blockers, and long‑term NSAIDs can reduce absorption.
• No significant interactions with most B12 formulations, but always disclose all supplements to your healthcare provider. | | **How It Works in the Body** | • B12 is bound to intrinsic factor (produced by parietal cells of the stomach) and absorbed in the terminal ileum.
• It serves as a co‑factor for methionine synthase (folate cycle) and for methylmalonyl‑CoA mutase (myelin synthesis). | | **Lab Tests to Check Levels** | • **Serum B12** (pg/mL).
• **Methylmalonic acid (MMA)** – rises when B12 is low.
• **Homocysteine** – elevated in B12 or folate deficiency. | | **Key Takeaway** | Vitamin B12 supplementation is safe, inexpensive, and effective for most people with deficiency. Choose the route/form that best matches the cause of deficiency and your convenience. | --- ### Practical Guidance | Scenario | Recommended Regimen | |----------|---------------------| | **Mild deficiency or prevention (e.g., vegetarian)** | Oral 250–500 µg daily (or 500 µg sublingual). | | **Severe deficiency or malabsorption** | IM 1000–2000 µg once weekly for 4–6 weeks, then 1000 µg monthly or 250–500 µg daily. | | **Pernicious anemia** | IM 1000 µg once daily for 1–2 weeks, then 1000 µg weekly for 2 weeks, then monthly. | | **Post‑surgery (e.g., gastric bypass)** | High‑dose oral (1000 µg/day) or IM, as prescribed. | | **Pregnancy** | 650 µg daily (often as part of prenatal vitamins). | > **Note** – The above dosages are general guidelines. Individual requirements vary, especially with chronic diseases, pregnancy, or very high‑dose therapies (e.g., certain cancer treatments). --- ### How to Choose a Product

**Vitamin D (Cholecalciferol, D3) – Treatment Overview** | Item | Details | |------|---------| | **What it is** | Vitamin D3 is a fat‑soluble secosteroid synthesized in the skin under UV‑B exposure and obtained from food or supplements. It is converted in the liver to 25‑hydroxyvitamin D₃ (25(OH)D₃), the circulating marker, and then in the kidney to the active 1,25‑di­hydroxyvitamin D₃ (1,25(OH)₂D₃). | | **Common Deficiency Symptoms** | Fatigue, muscle weakness, bone pain, osteopenia/osteoporosis, increased risk of fractures, impaired immunity, mood disturbances. | | **Assessment** | Serum 25(OH)D₃ < 20 ng/mL (50 nmol/L) is considered deficient; 20–30 ng/mL is insufficient. | | **Typical Treatment Regimens** | *Dosing is individualized and usually prescribed by a healthcare professional.* | | • **Loading dose** (if level < 10 ng/mL or severe deficiency) | 50 000 IU orally once a week **for 6–8 weeks** (or 100 000 IU weekly for 3–4 weeks in very low levels). | | • **Maintenance dose** (post‑loading or for mild deficiency) | 1 000–2 000 IU daily, or 50 000 IU weekly, or 600–800 IU daily for prevention. | | • **High‑dose therapy** (rare, for very low levels or malabsorption) | 200 000 IU orally **once** every 4–6 weeks for 6–8 weeks, then switch to a lower maintenance dose. | | • **Intramuscular (IM)** | 50 000 IU IM once weekly for 6–8 weeks is an alternative for patients unable to take oral supplements (e.g., severe malabsorption). | | **Formulations** | • Oral tablets (soft gels, capsules, tablets).
• Liquid drops (especially for infants, children, or patients who cannot swallow pills).
• Oral solutions (e.g., 1000 IU/mL, 2000 IU/mL). | | **Safety** | Vitamin D is generally safe; hypervitaminosis D is rare but can cause hypercalcemia, kidney stones, or calcification of soft tissues if dosages exceed 10 000 IU/day over a long period. | | **Monitoring** | Recheck serum 25(OH)D₃ after 6–8 weeks of loading dose or 3–6 months of maintenance to confirm adequacy and adjust dose. | | **Lifestyle Adjuncts** | • Safe sun exposure (10–30 min, 2–3 times weekly, depending on skin type and latitude).
• Dietary sources: fatty fish (salmon, mackerel), cod liver oil, egg yolks, fortified milk/juice, fortified cereals. | --- ### Practical “Start‑to‑Finish” Plan (Illustrative) 1. **Confirm deficiency**: Serum 25(OH)D₃ < 20 ng/mL. 2. **Initiate loading phase**: * 50 000 IU oral once weekly for 6 weeks (or 100 000 IU once weekly for 3 weeks if severe). * If oral intake is problematic, consider IM 50 000 IU weekly. 3. **Re‑measure** at week 6–8. 4. **Transition to maintenance**: * 1 000–2 000 IU daily (or 50 000 IU weekly) if serum > 30 ng/mL. * For prevention or mild deficiency, 600–800 IU daily is adequate. 5. **Monitor**: Repeat 25(OH)D₃ testing every 6–12 months or sooner if symptoms persist or risk factors change. --- ### Key Takeaways | Point | Why It Matters | |-------|----------------| | **Individualized dosing** | Vitamin D needs vary by age, baseline level, body weight, skin pigmentation, sun exposure, and comorbidities. | | **Loading dose** | Quickly corrects deficiency, especially important in osteoporosis or severe low levels. | | **Maintenance** | Prevents relapse; typical doses 1 000
